title: P2GC Federal Growth Review — Reusable Demo

fictionalCompany.name: Apex Ridge Solutions, LLC
fictionalCompany.focus: IT modernization, cybersecurity support, program support

scenes.title: Federal opportunities are everywhere. Clarity is not.
screen: A company can look healthy on paper and still have serious growth risk underneath the surface.
scenes.selfDiagnosis: Do you know which parts of your federal position are strong — and which only look strong?
scenes.visual: Fast-moving federal data tiles collapse into a clean P2GC intelligence view. Start confident, then reveal the line about hidden growth risk. Avatar only for opening 18 seconds, then transition to dashboard visual.
scenes.narration: Federal contractors rarely suffer from a lack of information. There are awards, forecasts, agency portals, GSA data, teaming opportunities and solicitations everywhere. The harder problem is knowing what those signals mean for your business. Why are you winning? Which revenue is exposed? Are your vehicles producing? Which opportunities actually deserve capture resources? A company can look healthy on paper and still have serious growth risk underneath the surface. The P2GC Federal Growth Review is designed to make that picture easier to see.

scenes.title: P2GC Federal Growth Review
screen: Federal data → Business meaning → Growth pathway
scenes.visual: Awards, GSA/VA, agencies, NAICS, recompetes, forecasts, competitors and opportunities flow into P2GC Intelligence, then Growth Diagnosis, then Growth Pathway.
scenes.narration: The Federal Growth Review connects information that normally sits in separate places. We examine current position, revenue exposure, vehicle use, agency buying patterns, competitive movement and realistic expansion paths. The objective is not to create the longest opportunity list. It is to turn disconnected federal information into business meaning — and then into a clearer growth pathway.

scenes.title: Current Federal Position + Federal Growth Scorecard
screen: How healthy, protected and scalable is your federal position?
scenes.selfDiagnosis: If one agency represents 40–50% of your federal revenue, do you know what happens if that work does not renew?
scenes.visual: Begin with strong five-year revenue growth and $4.2M current revenue. Then pivot to the scorecard. Show all scores clearly labeled fictional. Finish by isolating Overall Federal Growth Position: 60/100.
scenes.narration: Apex Ridge Solutions appears successful. It has 11.8 million dollars in five-year federal awards and about 4.2 million dollars in current annual federal revenue. Sixty-one percent is prime work. But half of current revenue comes from one agency. That is where confidence starts turning into questions. We summarize the fictional position in a scorecard: revenue stability 62, vehicle utilization 41, agency diversification 55, prime position 68, opportunity fit 74, and an overall federal growth position of 60 out of 100. These are demonstration scores, not real-company ratings. The question is not simply whether a company has federal business. The question is how healthy, protected and scalable that federal position really is.

scenes.title: Contract Vehicle ≠ Revenue
screen: A vehicle creates access. A strategy creates utilization.
Are we leaving usable access on the table?
scenes.selfDiagnosis: If you have a GSA Schedule, do you know whether it is actually producing at the level it should?
scenes.visual: Make the $4.2M versus $460K utilization comparison a major reveal. Add the fictional 41/100 vehicle-utilization score and a subtle 'underused?' callout. Include VA/VISN pathway reference where relevant.
scenes.narration: A contract vehicle can create access, but access is not the same as utilization. Apex Ridge has an active GSA Schedule with two relevant SINs, yet only about 460 thousand dollars of its 4.2 million dollars in annual federal revenue is flowing through that vehicle. That does not prove the Schedule is underperforming, but it creates an important business question: is existing access being used as effectively as it could be? Underused vehicles, weak buyer reach or poor positioning can represent revenue that is never pursued at all. If you already have a GSA Schedule, do you know what it is actually producing for you?

scenes.title: Revenue Exposure / Recompetes
screen: A company can look healthy — until you examine what is exposed.
64% of current revenue enters the exposure view
Protecting revenue can be as important as finding new revenue.
scenes.selfDiagnosis: Do you know which of your current awards may be recompeted, expire or require protection in the next 12–18 months?
scenes.visual: This is one of the strongest moments. Fill the screen with $4.2M CURRENT FEDERAL REVENUE, then visually carve out $2.7M POTENTIALLY EXPOSED WITHIN 18 MONTHS. Use an exposure timeline and three risk markers. Hold the $2.7M reveal long enough to register.
scenes.narration: Now the picture changes. Apex Ridge still has 4.2 million dollars in current federal revenue, but in this fictional scenario 2.7 million dollars is connected to contracts, option periods or buyer relationships that may need attention within the next 18 months. That is roughly 64 percent of the current revenue base entering an exposure view. Nothing here says the revenue will be lost. It says the company needs to know what requires protection, when recompetes are approaching, and where concentration creates dependency. Do you know which of your current awards may be recompeted or expire in the next 12 to 18 months?

scenes.title: Opportunity Environment
screen: The goal is not to find the most opportunities.
The goal is to identify the right opportunities for your company.
scenes.selfDiagnosis: Do you know which agencies are buying what you sell but have never bought from you — and which opportunities are actually worth your capture resources?
scenes.visual: Flood the screen with opportunity cards, then remove poor fits using Agency / NAICS / Vehicle / Past Performance / Prime-Sub / Timing / Buyer Fit. Finish with only seven qualified paths. Make discarded opportunities visibly fade away to communicate opportunity-cost discipline.
scenes.narration: This is where more information can actually become a problem. A contractor may see dozens or hundreds of possible pursuits, but every pursuit consumes time, capture effort and proposal resources. P2GC looks across active procurements, recompetes, forecasts, agency buying patterns, vehicles, prime opportunities, teaming paths, VA or VISN activity where relevant, and adjacent NAICS markets. Then we filter for fit. Does the company have relevant performance? Is the buyer already purchasing similar work? Is the route accessible? Is the timing realistic? In this example, dozens of possibilities become seven qualified paths. Poor pursuit selection can mean missing better opportunities while resources are tied up elsewhere. The goal is not the most opportunities. It is the right ones.

scenes.title: Competitive Position
screen: Competitors do not need your business to shrink for their position to strengthen.
scenes.selfDiagnosis: Are competitors winning work in agencies where you already have relevant past performance?
scenes.visual: Four-company comparison. Apex Ridge begins looking respectable, then competitors extend farther across agency reach, prime share and vehicle footprint. Highlight the gap without winner/loser hype.
scenes.narration: Performance also needs context. Apex Ridge is producing 4.2 million dollars annually, but several fictional peers are reaching more agencies and showing higher prime percentages. That does not automatically mean Apex Ridge is losing. It means competitors may be building position in places Apex Ridge has not yet reached. Are they monetizing vehicles more effectively? Entering agencies where Apex Ridge already has relevant past performance? Priming work Apex Ridge still performs as a subcontractor? Competitive movement matters because missed buying activity can become missed positioning long before a solicitation appears.

scenes.title: Federal Growth Gaps — What These Findings Could Mean
screen: 50% of revenue concentrated in one agency
Contract vehicles that may be underused
Agencies where expansion may make sense
Prime positions that could be strengthened
scenes.visual: Five growth-gap tiles connect into the Growth Diagnosis. Then transition those gaps into six practical implications under WHAT THESE FINDINGS COULD MEAN. This is the bridge from discomfort to clarity.
scenes.narration: Viewed together, the findings tell a much different story than the revenue number alone. Apex Ridge has real performance, but GSA may be underused, half of revenue sits in one agency, 2.7 million dollars may require protection, adjacent-buyer reach is limited, and prime position can improve. What could that mean? Revenue that deserves protection. A vehicle that may deserve more attention. Agencies where expansion may make sense. Prime positions that could be strengthened. Pursuits that deserve more capture resources — and others that should be ignored. For a contractor like this, correcting even one or two gaps could mean protecting existing revenue, improving use of an existing vehicle, expanding into additional buyers, or focusing resources on fewer but better-fit opportunities. No guaranteed wins — just better-informed decisions.

scenes.title: Protect → Expand → Capture
screen: PROTECT — Existing revenue / Recompetes / Key buyers
EXPAND — Adjacent agencies / Existing vehicles / Prime position
CAPTURE — Best-fit opportunities / Teaming paths / Priority pursuits
scenes.visual: Three-step pathway builds left to right. Tie each step visually back to an earlier risk: exposure → Protect, underused GSA/agency gap → Expand, filtered opportunities → Capture.
scenes.narration: That leads to the P2GC pathway: Protect, Expand and Capture. Protect the revenue and relationships already in place. Expand into logical agencies, buyers, vehicles and stronger prime positions. Then capture the opportunities with the best fit. The sequence matters because chasing every solicitation while existing revenue is exposed or positioning is weak can waste enormous effort. The purpose of the pathway is simple: know what deserves attention first, what should come next, and what should not consume resources at all.

What would this reveal about your company?
scenes.selfDiagnosis: What would this analysis reveal if the company on the screen were yours?
scenes.visual: Apex Ridge fades away and YOUR COMPANY replaces it. Flow: Company → Federal Intelligence → Growth Diagnosis → Recommended Pathway → Execution. End on a clean question: WHAT WOULD THIS REVEAL ABOUT YOUR COMPANY?
scenes.narration: Everything in this demonstration is fictional. With a real contractor, the same process is applied to that company's actual federal footprint. We examine the intelligence, connect the signals, identify what appears to deserve attention, and develop the recommended pathway. The demonstration shows how the analysis works. Your engagement applies that process to your actual company, priorities, opportunities and execution path. At this point, the most useful question is not what Apex Ridge should do. It is what this analysis would reveal about your company.
